variants.name: Thread interruption and Future.cancel(true)
variants.idiom_name: interrupt status flag + InterruptedException at blocking points
variants.implementation_notes: Java has no cancellation token object, so the local idiom replaces it: interruption carries the request on the thread. Thread.interrupt() sets the interrupt status, the blocking library methods (Thread.sleep, Object.wait, BlockingQueue.take, interruptible NIO) throw InterruptedException and clear it, and CPU-bound loops poll Thread.interrupted() (clears the flag) or isInterrupted() (does not). At the executor level Future.cancel(true) interrupts the running task when the implementation knows the thread, and shutdownNow() interrupts every task - while CompletableFuture.cancel does not interrupt the underlying computation at all. The consequence is a convention instead of a token: every layer must be interruption-aware and must restore or propagate the status.
pitfalls: Catching InterruptedException and returning normally without restoring the flag (Thread.currentThread().interrupt()) or rethrowing loses the request for the caller and for every layer above.
Future.cancel(false) only stops tasks that have not started; cancel(true) interrupts but still depends on the task observing it, and CompletableFuture.cancel does not interrupt running work.
InterruptedException and CancellationException are different signals: Future.get()/join() throw CancellationException for a cancelled task, so catching InterruptedException there is the wrong branch.

Work in an uninterruptible section (native I/O, an uninterruptible lock acquisition, a tight loop with no check) makes interruption invisible; prefer interruptible APIs and keep non-interruptible regions short and documented.

variants.name: StructuredTaskScope shutdown (preview)
variants.implementation_notes: Java 21's structured concurrency makes the task tree explicit: a StructuredTaskScope owns the subtasks forked into it, any subtask or the owner can call shutdown() to cancel the unfinished subtasks and stop new forks, ShutdownOnFailure/ShutdownOnSuccess implement the invoke-all/invoke-any policies, and joinUntil(Instant) enforces a deadline. Cancellation is still cooperative - shutdown interrupts the threads running the subtasks, so subtasks must be written to respond to interruption - and the scope is a preview API in JDK 21, so it must be enabled at compile and run time. Choose it when a task fans out into related subtasks whose lifetimes must be confined; keep the interrupt-based variant for plain executor code or older JDKs.
pitfalls: StructuredTaskScope is a preview API in JDK 21: code must compile and run with --enable-preview, and the API still changes between releases.
shutdown() cancels by interrupting: a subtask that ignores interrupts keeps running and makes join() wait, so every forked callable must be interruption-responsive.
Skipping join() before closing the scope makes close() wait for the subtasks and then fail with an exception, and calling Subtask.get() before joining throws instead of blocking.
